At the tea stall outside the polytechnic in Sagar, Dhruv, in his final year, waited for his junior Tushar with a notebook full of placement tips: aptitude tests, group discussions, the interview questions he'd faced.
Tushar arrived and pulled up a stool, and Dhruv caught himself. He had been about to hand over his own path. 'First tell me,' he said. 'What do you want, two years from now?'
Tushar hesitated. 'Honestly? Not a company job. I want to go back to our village and run my father's dairy better. Cold storage, maybe. Proper records.'
Dhruv closed the placement notebook. None of it fitted. 'Okay. Then your first internship should be at a dairy cooperative, not an IT firm. And we should look for the refrigeration elective.'
Tushar's face opened into a grin. 'Nobody ever asked me that before.'
They spent the next hour listing cooperatives within fifty kilometres.

Jaya, you asked how I mentor the first-years without it becoming a mess. This is Reena, and my one rule is: small pieces.
Last year my junior Kiran came to me and said, 'I want to learn programming.' That's like saying 'I want to learn the ocean.' So we broke it down. Every week: one concept, one exercise, one tiny program. Week one: variables, a quiz on types, and a program that greets you by name. Week two: conditions, three exercises, and a program that tells you if you've passed. Week three: loops, and a times-table printer.
Every Saturday at eleven we sat in the library and went through what Kiran wrote. Not what I would have written. What Kiran wrote.
By week ten, Kiran had built a small attendance tracker for the class. Nobody had to learn the ocean. Just one bucket at a time.

qa.a: Tell you if you've passed.

qa.a: Reena sounds confident and proud of the method, joking about learning the ocean one bucket at a time.

Week one: printing and variables, five exercises, a program that prints your timetable. Week two: if-else, a grade calculator. And so on, for eight weeks.

Hi Dolma,
Thanks for sending your code. I know you want me to just tell you what's wrong, and I could. But I think you'll get more out of it this way.
Before I look closely, can you answer three things?
1. What have you tried so far? Even the things that didn't work.
2. What does the error message say, word for word? Which line does it point to?
3. What did you expect that line to do, and what does it actually do? Try printing the value just before that line.
Send me your answers tonight. If you're still stuck after that, I'll give you a hint, a small one, I promise. I'm not being difficult. When I was in first year, my senior did this to me, and I was annoyed for a week, and then I found I could debug on my own.
Talk soon,
Hrithik

In a café near the university in Ankara, Rafael, a first-year exchange student from Brazil, admitted he was thinking of skipping the internship coding test. 'Everyone else is better. I'll freeze and fail.'
Elif, his mentor, stirred her tea. She thought about giving him tips. Instead she decided to tell him the truth.
'In my second year I failed the first coding round at the company where I'm now interning. Completely. I solved zero out of three. I froze on the first question, panicked, and wasted forty minutes.'
Rafael stared. 'You? But you're...'
'I practised timed problems every week after that. I learned to skip a question I'm stuck on. I applied again the next year and passed.' She shrugged. 'That fear you have? I had it too. It's normal. It doesn't mean you'll fail. It means it matters to you.'
Rafael sat back. 'Okay. Maybe I'll take it. And practise with a timer first.'

Hi Sahil,
Our first two meetings were great, but I've seen mentoring fizzle out before: lots of energy in week one, then everyone gets busy and it just stops. So I'd like us to fix a simple routine now.
1. A 20-minute call every Sunday at 7 p.m. If one of us can't make it, we move it to Monday, not skip it.
2. A shared notes file with three headings: Goals, Next steps, Doubts. I've already started it and added your goal of getting a data internship by May.
3. Before each call, you update 'Next steps' with what you did and 'Doubts' with anything confusing. I'll read it before we talk, so we don't waste time.
That's it. It shouldn't take more than half an hour a week for either of us. If it isn't working after a month, we'll change it.
Excited to see where this goes!
Noor

In the small college in Bagalkot, Jahnavi had been mentoring Tejas in spoken English and interview skills since June. Every week she gave him two things: a short article to read aloud and five practice questions to answer in writing.
In August he stopped doing them. Three weeks in a row, the notebook came back blank. Jahnavi felt a flicker of irritation, then decided to ask instead of assuming.
'Tejas, what's happening? No blame.'
He looked at the floor. 'Harvest season, akka. I'm in the fields with my father from six till college, and after college till dark. And the semester exams start in two weeks.'
Jahnavi hadn't known about the harvest at all. 'Okay. For the next two weeks, forget the articles. Just one practice question each week, and you can answer it aloud to me after class instead of writing.'
Tejas let out a breath. 'That I can do.'
After exams and harvest, the notebook started filling up again.
